analysis.one_liner: Protects about 5.7 million acres of Utah desert canyon country as roadless federal wilderness.
analysis.headline: The bill to designate about 5.7 million acres of Utah wilderness went to a House subcommittee in April 1993 and never received a markup or floor vote before that Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would add dozens of named wilderness units on Bureau of Land Management land in Utah to the National Wilderness Preservation System, from the Great Basin ranges to the Book Cliffs, permanently protecting them from new roads, motorized use, and most commercial development. It also reserves federal water rights for each area to keep streams flowing for the wilderness. The bill never got past committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans who hike, hunt, fish, paddle, and photograph on public land, plus anyone who values Utah's canyon country, wildlife, and Anasazi archaeological sites staying unroaded and undeveloped.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hikers, hunters, anglers, and public-land visitors

how_it_helps.text: The bill designates wilderness across ten Utah regions — Great Basin, Zion and Mojave Desert, Grand Staircase and Kaiparowits Plateau, Escalante Canyons, Henry Mountains, Dirty Devil River, Cedar Mesa, Canyonlands, San Rafael Swell, and Book Cliffs and Uinta Basin — with the tables in the bill totaling roughly 5.7 million acres.

Wilderness status permanently bars new road construction, motorized vehicles, and most commercial development on these lands, while preserving hiking, hunting, grazing under existing rights, and access to archaeological sites such as the Cedar Mesa cliff dwellings.

The bill reserves a quantity of federal water sufficient for each wilderness area, with the priority date of enactment, and directs the Interior Secretary to file claims in Utah stream adjudications to protect stream flows into the wilderness.

Existing rights are respected: the wilderness areas are administered 'subject to valid existing rights,' and the bill states it does not reduce any water rights already held by the United States in Utah.

analysis.who_pays: Mining, oil and gas, and grazing operators who could no longer prospect, build roads, or develop most of these lands, and off-highway-vehicle users who lose motorized routes. Utah water users could also face new senior federal water claims in court.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mining, oil, gas, grazing, and OHV interests

drawbacks.text: Designation locks these lands into a roadless condition with no motorized access or new development, which opponents in Utah argued took away local economic opportunities and county control over how nearby public land is used.

The reserved federal water rights carry an enactment-date priority and must be quantified in Utah's courts, which could place the federal government ahead of future state-based water users in over-subscribed basins.

The proposal was far larger than what Congress eventually agreed to consider for Utah, so its full scope would have taken far more acreage out of multiple-use management than any competing plan on the table.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is permanent protection of some of the largest remaining roadless desert in the lower 48 states — scenery, wildlife habitat, and archaeology that cannot be recreated once roads and drilling go in. The costs are real but narrow: forgone mineral development, restricted motorized access, and a federal water reservation that could complicate Utah water administration on those specific drainages. On the whole, the trade favors a broad, dispersed public benefit over concentrated private uses of the same land.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its National Parks, Forests and Public Lands subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Maurice Hinchey introduced the bill on March 25, 1993 with 16 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the same day.
It gathered 94 cosponsors in total: 84 Democrats, 9 Republicans, and 1 Independent.

On April 13, 1993 it was referred to the Subcommittee on National Parks, Forests and Public Lands, and the action record shows no further action — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — through the end of the 103rd Congress on January 3, 1995.

The bill would have designated wilderness in ten Utah regions, from the Great Basin to the Book Cliffs, with the acreage tables in the bill text adding up to about 5.7 million acres, and reserved federal water rights for each area.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, mining, oil and gas, grazing, and off-road-vehicle interests kept the status quo: the lands stayed open to multiple use with no wilderness restrictions and no federal reserved water claims. Wilderness supporters gained nothing from this Congress.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the Utah BLM Wilderness Act of 1993 on March 25, 1993.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a small bipartisan base.

for.name: Conservation groups backing a large Utah wilderness designation
for.what_they_did: Publicly pushed for the citizens' proposal to designate roughly 5.7 million acres of Utah BLM land as wilderness.

against.name: House Natural Resources Subcommittee on National Parks, Forests and Public Lands
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 13, 1993 and never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill died there.

against.name: Utah's congressional delegation
against.what_they_did: Opposed the 5.7-million-acre designation and promoted a far smaller, state-preferred wilderness proposal for Utah.

against.name: Mining, oil and gas, and grazing operators
against.role: Extractive and grazing interests on the affected lands
against.what_they_did: Opposed wilderness designation of the BLM lands, which would bar new mineral entry, road construction, and expanded development.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic — 84 of 94 cosponsors — with 9 Republicans and 1 Independent; no roll-call vote ever occurred because the bill never left subcommittee.

industries.industry: Hardrock mining and oil and gas companies
industries.note: Wilderness designation bars new mineral entry, road construction, and most development across roughly 5.7 million acres of BLM land, ending prospecting and drilling potential there. The bill's gain to the public — permanent protection of roadless land — is precisely what these companies lose.

The bill reserves federal water for each wilderness area with an enactment-date priority and requires the Interior Secretary to file quantification claims in Utah's stream adjudications, potentially creating senior federal claims ahead of future state water users. The federal reservation protects wilderness stream flows, which is the public's interest.

industries.industry: Off-highway vehicle and motorized recreation users
industries.note: Wilderness closes these lands to motorized travel and new routes. This is a genuine loss for a segment of the public, though motorized users are a concentrated user group rather than a commercial industry.
Grazing under valid existing rights may continue in wilderness, but operators lose flexibility for new range facilities, water developments, and expanded operations on designated land.
Permanent protection of canyon-country scenery, wildlife, and archaeological sites supports outfitting, guiding, and visitation economies that depend on intact public land.
